security.meta.title: Security & Privacy - encrypt.click
security.meta.description: How encrypt.click handles data: browser-side crypto, encrypted chat and transfers, what third parties see, and what we do not collect.
security.subtitle: A plain-language summary of how encrypt.click is designed to handle your data. For information only - not legal advice.
security.noAccounts.title: No accounts, no logins
security.noAccounts.text: encrypt.click has no user accounts, logins, or profiles. You do not need to register or provide personal information to use the tools.
security.clientSide.title: Browser-side tools
security.clientSide.p1: The privacy tools, such as AES words, Time capsule, Steganography, Photo cipher and Spectral cipher, run in your browser using Web Crypto and other browser APIs. Their inputs are not uploaded to encrypt.click for processing.
security.clientSide.p2: When a tool requests public data at your direction, such as drand randomness for Time Capsule through our same-origin proxy, the request does not include your plaintext secrets or passwords.
security.shortening.title: Link shortening
security.shortening.p1: Links are not shortened unless you ask. When you press Shorten link, your browser sends the share link to /api/shorten on encrypt.click, which shortens it with our own service at l.encrypt.click. No third-party shorteners are used. If shortening fails, you keep the full link.
security.shortening.p2: The short link stores the full link including the encrypted payload, but never the password. Anyone with the short link still needs the password, so use the generated passphrase or another strong password.
security.shortening.p3: Only then is the encrypted payload stored on l.encrypt.click. The full link carries the payload in the URL fragment, which the recipient's browser never sends to a server.
security.cookies.title: Cookies and browser storage
security.cookies.p1: The site sets one functional cookie, ec-lang, only after you pick a language in the menu. It holds the two-letter language code, nothing else, for one year, and is not used for tracking. The first visit without it is served in your browser language. Your browser may use localStorage for the theme and, where chat history is kept, encrypted messages, in saved rooms also how far each member's history has been checked. Session storage may briefly hold a room password while you join, and keeps a room key that arrived in a link for as long as that tab is open, so the key can leave the address bar. IndexedDB holds the signing key your browser creates for each chat room and whiteboard and, for saved rooms, the seed of the post-quantum signing key, sealed under a key derived from the room link; the private keys never leave the device. If you save rooms under My rooms, IndexedDB also keeps their names, modes and visit times as they are, and their passwords or links only encrypted under a key that only your passkey can release.
security.cookies.p2: Cloudflare (hosting) may set cookies for security and abuse prevention depending on traffic and browser settings, under Cloudflare's own policies.
security.network.title: Network and transport security
security.network.li1: All traffic is served over HTTPS with modern TLS.
security.network.li2: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is enabled with includeSubDomains and preload.
security.network.li3: Content Security Policy (CSP) restricts scripts, styles, fonts, and connections; inline script hashes are used instead of broad unsafe-inline for scripts.
security.network.li4: Framing is disabled via frame-ancestors 'none' and X-Frame-Options: DENY.
security.thirdParty.title: Third-party infrastructure
security.thirdParty.p1: The site runs on Cloudflare Workers. Real-time chat and the whiteboard are relayed by Durable Objects in the same Worker (PartyServer). Calls may be relayed through Cloudflare TURN or another configured TURN provider. Temporary ciphertext hosts, including Send-compatible instances, may receive encrypted blobs when first-party upload is unavailable.
security.thirdParty.p2: encrypt.click does not maintain a database of your tool inputs. API abuse controls use a salted hash of the IP address held in memory for about 60 seconds. Cloudflare may also apply bot detection or challenges under its own policies. Our Content-Security-Policy blocks the inline bot-detection script Cloudflare can add to pages, so it does not run next to your keys.
security.disclosure.title: Responsible disclosure
security.disclosure.text: If you believe you found a security or privacy issue in encrypt.click, email mail@encrypt.click. Include enough detail to reproduce the issue and avoid testing that could impact other users.
security.nonLegal.title: Non-legal summary
security.nonLegal.text: This page is a human-readable summary of how encrypt.click is designed to handle data. It is not a contract or a complete set of legal terms. Perfect security cannot be guaranteed; you use the tools at your own risk.

tools.about.title: How it works
tools.photoCipher.about.1.title: What it does
tools.photoCipher.about.1: Photo cipher hides an encrypted message inside an ordinary photo in a way designed to survive moderate JPEG recompression, which is what chat apps and social networks do to images. The person who receives the photo opens it here with the same password and gets the message back.
tools.photoCipher.about.2.title: How the message is hidden
tools.photoCipher.about.2: The photo is split into 8×8 pixel blocks, the same grid JPEG works on. Each block carries one bit by nudging its average brightness to the nearest even or odd step on a scale of 24 levels, a technique called quantization index modulation that Brian Chen and Gregory Wornell described around 1998. JPEG compression keeps the average brightness of a block quite well, so the bits tend to survive. Every bit is written 7 times in blocks spread across the picture, and a majority vote corrects damaged copies.
tools.photoCipher.about.3.title: Encryption and capacity
tools.photoCipher.about.3: Before hiding, the message is encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a key derived from your password with Argon2id (64 MiB of memory, 3 passes). The photo is scaled so that its sides are between 800 and 2,048 pixels. Capacity is small: an 800×800 photo holds roughly 78 characters, and larger photos hold more.
tools.photoCipher.about.4.title: Limits
tools.photoCipher.about.4: Resizing, cropping, filters, brightness changes or very strong compression destroy the hidden data, and some apps downscale large photos automatically. Send the photo as a file when you can and test it first. The brightness changes may show up as faint blockiness on smooth areas such as sky. The hiding pattern is public, so anyone with this tool can tell that a photo carries data; only the content is protected, by your password. Everything runs in your browser and the photo is not uploaded.
tools.spectralCipher.about.1.title: What it does
tools.spectralCipher.about.1: Spectral cipher draws a picture into sound. It turns an image into a WAV file that sounds like noise, but when you open the audio in a spectrogram viewer, which plots frequencies over time, the picture appears. The reveal mode does the reverse and extracts the image from such a WAV file.
tools.spectralCipher.about.2.title: A musical trick
tools.spectralCipher.about.2: Musicians have hidden images in spectrograms for decades. Aphex Twin put his own grinning face into a track on the 1999 Windowlicker single, Nine Inch Nails hid images in the Year Zero album in 2007, and Mick Gordon tucked pentagrams and the number 666 into the 2016 Doom soundtrack.
tools.spectralCipher.about.3.title: How it works
tools.spectralCipher.about.3: The image is resized to 512×512 pixels and turned to grayscale. Each column becomes a short slice of sound of about 46 ms, and each row becomes a frequency between 300 Hz and 14 kHz whose loudness follows the brightness of the pixel. The result, about 24 seconds long, is mixed into a carrier track; the strength slider sets how strongly the image stands out against it.
tools.spectralCipher.about.4.title: Good to know
tools.spectralCipher.about.4: This is a hidden picture, not encryption. There is no password, and anyone who opens the file in a spectrogram viewer such as Audacity will see the image. Use it for puzzles, art and fun, not for secrets. MP3 and AAC compression, resampling or trimming the start can blur or shift the image, so share the WAV as it is. Everything runs in your browser.
tools.steganography.about.1.title: What it does
tools.steganography.about.1: This tool hides an encrypted message inside a PNG image. The picture looks the same to the eye, but someone with the password can pull the message back out here. It is handy when you want a secret to travel as an innocent-looking image.
tools.steganography.about.2.title: An ancient idea
tools.steganography.about.2: Steganography means covered writing in Greek. Herodotus tells of Histiaeus, who around 500 BC shaved a slave's head, tattooed a message on the scalp and sent him off once the hair had grown back. The German abbot Johannes Trithemius gave the craft its name in his book Steganographia, written in 1499. Invisible ink and microdots continued the tradition, and digital images are its modern form.
tools.steganography.about.3.title: How it works
tools.steganography.about.3: The message is first encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with a key derived from your password with Argon2id (64 MiB of memory, 3 passes). The encrypted bits are then written into the least significant bit of the red, green and blue values of each pixel, starting at the top left. Changing a colour value by one out of 255 is invisible. Each pixel holds 3 bits, so even a small image can carry a long message.
tools.steganography.about.4.title: Limits
tools.steganography.about.4: The hidden data survives only an exact copy of the PNG file. Any resizing, cropping, editing or conversion to JPEG, which most chat apps and social networks do, wipes it out; send the file as a document or attachment, or use Photo cipher instead. The method is simple, and statistical tools can detect that an image carries data, even though they cannot read it without the password. Everything runs in your browser and nothing is uploaded.
tools.timeCapsule.about.1.title: What it does
tools.timeCapsule.about.1: Time capsule locks a message until a moment you choose. Before that time nobody can open it: not the recipient, not you and not encrypt.click. Afterwards, anyone with the capsule can. It suits sealed predictions, delayed reveals, contest answers or a letter to your future self.
tools.timeCapsule.about.2.title: drand and the League of Entropy
tools.timeCapsule.about.2: The lock is opened by drand, a public randomness beacon that grew out of research at the Swiss university EPFL. Since 2019 it has been run by the League of Entropy, a group of independent organisations that agreed to operate it together. Founders included Cloudflare, Protocol Labs, Kudelski Security, the University of Chile and EPFL, and today the network includes the Ethereum Foundation, University College London and more than a dozen others. Every 3 seconds the members jointly produce a threshold BLS signature for the next round number. No single member, and no small group of them, can create it alone or ahead of time.
tools.timeCapsule.about.3.title: How the lock works
tools.timeCapsule.about.3: Your chosen time is converted to a future drand round. The message is encrypted in your browser with tlock, a scheme published by drand researchers in 2023: identity-based encryption on the BLS12-381 curve, where the round number is the identity and the beacon's future signature for that round is the only key that opens it. Inside, the message is packed in the age format and sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305. Encrypting needs nothing secret from anyone; decrypting needs the signature, which does not exist until the round arrives.
tools.timeCapsule.about.4.title: A short history of timelocks
tools.timeCapsule.about.4: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and David Wagner proposed time-lock puzzles in 1996: problems that take a known amount of sequential computing to solve. Rivest's LCS35 puzzle, set at MIT in 1999 and expected to take 35 years, was cracked in 2019 by the Belgian programmer Bernard Fabrot after three and a half years of computing on a home PC. Puzzles like that depend on how fast computers get. tlock depends on a clock run by many organisations instead, so the unlock time is accurate to a few seconds.
tools.timeCapsule.about.5.title: Good to know
tools.timeCapsule.about.5: A password is optional. Without one, anyone with the capsule can read it after the unlock time; with one, they also need that password, which nobody can recover for you. The unlock time itself is visible inside the capsule. Your browser reaches drand through encrypt.click's server, which forwards requests to api.drand.sh. It sees which round is requested, never your message, and your browser checks every beacon's signature, so the server cannot fake one. If drand shut down before your round, the capsule could never be opened. Opening early would require a large share of the League's members to collude. The time lock is not resistant to future quantum computers: one could open a capsule early, unless it also has a password, which Argon2id and AES-256 protect as long as it is strong.
chat.about.1.title: How to start
chat.about.1: Choose how messages are kept, pick a room name, set a password of at least 16 characters that is hard to guess and share the link with the people you want to talk to. Rooms are created only here, so every room gets a strong password and an explicit message mode; opening the address of a room that does not exist leads back to this form. The link does not carry the key: everyone has to type the password, which you should share another way, for example in person or over a different app.
chat.about.2.title: Messages
chat.about.2: Every message is encrypted in your browser with AES-256-GCM. When you join, the password goes through Argon2id once, with 64 MiB of memory and 3 passes, so every offline guess is slow and memory-hungry. HKDF-SHA256 then splits the result into the message key, which also depends on the room's message mode, and a second, separate value that only proves to the server that you belong in the room. The server learns that value, never the encryption key, and the room on the server is named after a hash of it rather than after your room name. Every message also gets a second layer with forward secrecy, described below.
chat.about.3.title: What the server sees and keeps
chat.about.3: Rooms run on Cloudflare Workers. The relay forwards encrypted messages to the people in the room and does not store them. It keeps only the room settings, and deletes them when the room has been empty for 7 days. It does see when messages are sent, how many people are connected and, from the timing, when someone is probably typing. Every message is padded to one of a limited set of sizes, at least 512 bytes, so short messages and typing indicators look the same and longer ones only show their rough size. Presence signals and key exchanges carry post-quantum keys, so they are larger and the relay can tell them from short messages by size. Cloudflare, like any host, sees your IP address, and the room name appears in the page address you load.
chat.about.4.title: History and disappearing messages
chat.about.4: In the default mode each participant keeps the history in their own browser: the signed messages, sealed under a key derived from the room secret, so they survive a reload. Members who are online hand up to the last 200 messages to a newcomer, encrypted for that newcomer alone and still carrying every author's signature, so nobody can put words in someone else's mouth while passing history on. Forward secrecy protects what crosses the relay; what members' browsers keep, they can show anyone who joins with the password, which is what this mode is for. You can instead make all messages disappear between 5 seconds and a day after they are shown, and then nothing is kept. In any room, ending a single message with !N, such as !30, makes just that message disappear after N seconds, and it is left out of the stored history. The timer runs in each participant's browser, so a modified client or a simple screenshot can still keep a copy.
chat.about.5.title: Calls
chat.about.5: Voice and video calls use WebRTC. On top of its standard DTLS-SRTP encryption, your browser encrypts every audio and video frame, screen sharing included, with AES-256-GCM before it leaves, in the style of SFrame. Each participant creates a random media key on joining and gives it to every other participant separately: inside the encrypted room channel, sealed once more with a key only those two browsers share for this call (ECDH P-256 + ML-KEM-768). When someone leaves, everyone who stays switches to a new key, so whoever left cannot decrypt what follows. Frames that do not decrypt are dropped, never played, and a browser that cannot encrypt frames cannot join a call. Call setup travels through the room as encrypted messages. Media always goes through a TURN relay, so participants never see each other's IP addresses; the relay only forwards encrypted packets. Every participant connects to every other one, so calls work best in small groups.
chat.about.6.title: Files
chat.about.6: Files up to 128 MB are encrypted in your browser with a random key of their own, including the file name. The key and the download link travel only inside the encrypted message, so a file is protected exactly like the message that carries it, forward secrecy included. The encrypted file is uploaded to encrypt.click's own storage, or, if that fails, to backup hosts through encrypt.click's server (files up to 50 MB only). The hosts see only the encrypted file, its size and the uploading address. Uploaded files are deleted 24 hours after upload; the message stays in the history, the download does not.
chat.about.7.title: Good to know
chat.about.7: The chat is only as private as the password: anyone who has it can join and read along from then on. A password learned later does not open traffic recorded before, although in the default mode members who are online pass recent history on to whoever joins. A different password under the same room name is a separate private group that others never see, so if the page says the room does not exist although you expected others there, check the password. Up to 32 people can join a room.
chat.about.8.title: Member keys
chat.about.8: In every room your browser creates a signing key for that room and keeps it to itself; every message carries the public half and a signature, and anything unsigned is dropped, including history that other members pass on. Names are only labels: the random alias or whatever a member typed. Other members remember which key a name first appeared with and warn you when the same name, or one that only looks like it, shows up under a new key, which is what an impostor who knows the password would look like. The members panel shows a key code for each member, a short fingerprint of that one key, and a safety number derived from both your keys, which is the same on both screens: compare it in person or by voice. A new browser or device gets a new key, so expect that warning after you switch. The signature proves who in the room wrote a message, not who they are, and the password is still the only thing that lets someone in. The message mode is part of the room key, so the server cannot quietly turn a room with disappearing messages into one that keeps history. The key mark shows as four emoji and the safety number as seven emoji picked from a set of 64 symbols, covering 24 and 42 bits of the key fingerprints — enough to catch a casual mix-up, not a determined attacker, so compare them by voice or in person when it matters.
chat.about.9.title: Forward secrecy
chat.about.9: In every room the room key alone opens no message. Each browser creates fresh P-256 and ML-KEM-768 key pairs when it joins and keeps them in memory only. Every member has its own sending chain: each message is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key that HKDF-SHA256 derives from the chain, then the chain moves one step on and used keys are deleted. Every other member gets the current chain key separately, sealed under a key made from their two ephemeral keys (ECDH), a fresh ML-KEM-768 secret and a secret derived from the room password, inside the signed room channel as always. Someone who records the traffic and learns the password later cannot read the messages without breaking the key exchange, and once the session is over the keys needed are on no device any more. A future quantum computer that breaks P-256 would also have to break ML-KEM-768, so a recording stays closed even to someone who knows the password. Chains are replaced after 100 messages or 10 minutes and whenever someone leaves: the new chain goes only to members who answer, so whoever left cannot read on with the keys they had. Newcomers get each chain only at its current step, so nothing that crossed the relay before they arrived opens with their keys.
chat.about.10.title: My rooms
chat.about.10: Once you are in a room, the bookmark button next to the room link adds it to My rooms, a list shown on this page. It stays in this browser on this device and is never synced or sent anywhere. The room name, the label you give it, its mode and the time of your last visit are stored as they are, the same facts your browser history already holds. The password is stored only encrypted with AES-256-GCM, under a key that HKDF-SHA256 derives from the output of the WebAuthn PRF extension of a passkey created for this list, so only that passkey, unlocked with your fingerprint, face, PIN or security key, can release it. The key lives in memory for the open page only and is never stored. Where the browser or passkey cannot produce that output, the list keeps names only and you enter the password again. Forget removes one room; Forget everything removes the list and the passkey reference, while the passkey itself is deleted in your device or password manager.

whiteboard.about.1.title: How to start
whiteboard.about.1: Pick a room name, keep the generated passphrase or type your own of at least 16 characters that is hard to guess, and open the board. Send the link to your collaborators and share the password separately, ideally in person or over another app; the password is not part of the link.
whiteboard.about.2.title: Encryption
whiteboard.about.2: The password goes through Argon2id once, with 64 MiB of memory, 3 passes and a salt made from the room name, and HKDF-SHA256 splits the result into a base key and a separate value that lets you into the room without revealing the key to the server. Every stroke, shape, text and cursor movement is padded and encrypted in your browser before it leaves, each message with its own AES-256-GCM key derived from the base key and a fresh random salt, so even hours of busy cursor traffic never wear out a single key.
whiteboard.about.3.title: What the server sees and keeps
whiteboard.about.3: The relay on Cloudflare Workers passes encrypted updates between participants. It stores nothing: the drawing lives only in the browsers of the people in the room and syncs between them as encrypted CRDT updates, so when the last person leaves, the board is gone unless someone exported it. The relay sees how many people are connected, when updates are sent and how large they are, and Cloudflare sees IP addresses.
whiteboard.about.4.title: Good to know
whiteboard.about.4: Anyone with the room name and password can join and see everything on the board, so treat them like a key. A different password under the same board name is a separate private group that others never see. Up to 32 people can draw together, and anyone in the room can lock it so that nobody new can join until they unlock it or leave. The board also has its own encrypted chat. Its messages travel with the drawing, so newcomers see recent ones; they vanish when the last person leaves. End a message with !N to make it disappear after N seconds.
whiteboard.about.5.title: Signatures and keys
whiteboard.about.5: Each browser also keeps its own signing key for every board. Everything you send, from strokes and cursor moves to chat messages, is stamped with the room, the time and a unique id and signed with that key before it is encrypted, so nobody in the room can speak under someone else's name and the relay cannot replay old updates. The first key seen with a name is trusted; if the same or a lookalike name later shows up with a different key, it is marked as a new key on the cursor and in the chat. Open the people list in the bottom bar to compare safety numbers and trust the key.

security.chat.title: Encrypted chat, calls, whiteboard, and files
security.chat.p1: Chat messages, typing indicators, and call signaling are encrypted in the browser (AES-GCM) before they reach the relay. The relay forwards ciphertext and does not store chat message history, except for saved rooms, where it keeps the encrypted messages (at most 1000 per room, in the European Union) until a member deletes the room or it has gone unvisited for 90 days. In rooms without server history, messages also have forward secrecy: each member's sending key moves on with every message and reaches the others only under keys from short-lived key pairs that are never stored, so recorded traffic stays closed even to someone who learns the password later.
security.chat.p2: Live calls use WebRTC with a TURN-only ICE policy so peer IP addresses are not exchanged directly. Besides DTLS-SRTP, every audio and video frame is end-to-end encrypted in the browser with AES-256-GCM (SFrame-style insertable streams, VP8 or VP9 for video). Each sender's media key is random, travels only inside the encrypted and signed room channel, is sealed again for each recipient with ephemeral P-256 (ECDH) and ML-KEM-768 keys, and is replaced whenever a participant leaves. Because media keys never pass through the DTLS handshake, recording call traffic now and breaking that handshake later, for example with a quantum computer, does not expose the media to anyone who lacks the room secret. Browsers without frame encryption cannot join calls. TURN credentials are fetched from encrypt.click (/api/turn).
security.chat.p3: Chat file attachments are encrypted in the browser before upload, the same way as in Encrypt & share. They go to our own storage and are deleted after 24 hours, even in saved rooms. When our storage is unavailable, the encrypted file goes to a public Send instance in the EU instead, where it can stay for up to 7 days.
security.chat.p4: New rooms always need a password of at least 16 characters that passes a strength check, and they can only be created through the create form. The password is never part of the link, so share it separately.

security.share.title: Encrypted message and file sharing
security.share.p1: Encrypt & share runs AES-GCM in your browser before anything is uploaded. The password stays on your device unless you copy or send it yourself.
security.share.p2: Automatic upload prefers first-party ciphertext storage (this site's /upload). That path accepts up to about 128 MB — sealed in the browser — with a monthly budget, and the file is kept for 1 hour, 24 hours or 7 days, as you choose. One-time download still applies. If first-party storage is full or unavailable and the share uses the default settings (24 hours, any number of downloads) with a file under 50 MB, you are asked first; if you agree, your browser posts ciphertext only to encrypt.click's upload API, which relays it server-side to temporary Send-compatible hosts. Those hosts should see ciphertext and server egress - not a direct browser upload of plaintext.
security.share.p3: Recipients open links on encrypt.click (often /u). Encrypted material may sit in the URL fragment (not sent to our servers on normal page loads) or point at uploaded ciphertext. Optional PNG wrapping can hide the share link in an image for offline handoff. The receive page can also read a QR code with the camera or from a picture. Decoding runs on your device, and a share link for this site opens with its payload in the URL fragment, so the payload is not sent to the server.
security.share.p4: Uploads are free, so automated or unusually heavy use is checked. Normal uploads go through without anything extra; when an upload looks automated or a device has uploaded a lot, the browser first has to solve a short proof-of-work puzzle. It runs on your device and involves no third party. Each further puzzle within the hour takes twice as long, and a solved one lets that device keep uploading for an hour, within the same hard daily limits.
security.share.p5: The server stores each upload with its expiry time and refuses it from then on, even before storage deletes it. With one-time download it hands the file out once: the first request claims it atomically, every later request is refused, and the file is deleted as soon as it has been sent. Whoever opens the link first gets the file, so send such links only over a channel you trust. The expiry time and the one-time setting are also written into the link in readable form, so the recipient sees them before entering the password; they reveal nothing about the content.
security.chat.p5: Whiteboards use the same realtime infrastructure. A live board is relayed and never stored. A saved board keeps its encrypted changes and snapshots on the server, in the European Union and up to 16 MB, until a member deletes it or it has gone unvisited for 90 days; its key is a random value in the link fragment, which never reaches the server. Pictures are embedded in the board's encrypted document instead of being uploaded. Treat a live board's password or a saved board's link like a key.
security.chat.p6: Saved rooms use a random key carried in the link fragment, which never reaches the server. In every room, each message is signed in the browser with a per-room key, so other members can tell when a name turns up under a different key, and the message mode is bound into the room key, so the server cannot change it. Saved rooms add an ML-DSA-44 signature to every message and chain each author's stored messages, so browsers notice when the server leaves out, reorders or holds back messages.
security.network.li5: The deployment check compares freshly fetched assets and the build manifest from this server. It cannot prove the authenticity of the code running in your browser or protect against a compromised host.

tools.chatCipher.about.1.title: What it does
tools.chatCipher.about.1: Chat cipher encrypts your message with a password, then writes the ciphertext as a string of casual Czech chat messages. Paste that cover text back here with the same password to recover the original.
tools.chatCipher.about.2.title: The encryption
tools.chatCipher.about.2: Your password is stretched with Argon2id and a random salt into a 256-bit key. The message is sealed with AES-256-GCM. A wrong password or a changed cover text fails closed instead of returning garbage.
tools.chatCipher.about.3.title: Chat cover text
tools.chatCipher.about.3: The cover comes from a word table counted from about 60 million words of generated Czech chat (Mercury 3, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, DeepSeek, GLM-5.3 and others). It needs no model or GPU and writes a cover in milliseconds. Ciphertext bits choose the next words, with likely words coming up more often, so the result reads like someone typing a burst of messages. The constant bytes of the envelope are left out, so covers do not open alike. Expect a long cover even for a short secret, because salt, nonce and tag always travel with it.
tools.chatCipher.about.4.title: Download and privacy
tools.chatCipher.about.4: The word table is fetched only from this site, never from third-party hosts, and stays in this browser’s cache. Once it has loaded, encrypting and decrypting do not contact the network. Clearing site data removes it.
tools.chatCipher.about.5.title: Good to know
tools.chatCipher.about.5: The cover looks like chat to a casual reader and often drifts between topics. A trained detector can still tell it is machine-written, but without the password nobody can prove a message is inside. Use a long passphrase. Accents, capitals and small typos do not matter, but keep the punctuation or line breaks between words. Covers written by the older Kecal and Falcon models cannot be opened here. The cover is always Czech; other languages are not supported yet.

security.share.p6: A share can also be locked until a chosen time. The browser creates a random 32-byte secret, locks it to the matching drand round with tlock (the scheme behind Time capsule) and puts the locked secret in the link. The key that opens the message is derived with HKDF-SHA256 from both the password-derived key and that secret, so the password alone opens nothing before the drand network publishes the round, and the beacon alone opens nothing without the password. Uploaded files are kept until at least an hour after they unlock, so the unlock time can be at most 7 days away; a short message inside the link has no such limit. The round number, and with it the unlock time, is readable in the link.

security.share.p7: If you install encrypt.click as an app, it appears in your device's share sheet. Files, text and links you share to it there are caught by the site's service worker on your device and placed in the share form. They are not sent to the server, and nothing is encrypted or uploaded until you continue.

whiteboard.about.6.title: Backups
whiteboard.about.6: Export board in the board menu saves the whole board, drawings, pictures and board chat included, as a file you can bring back with Import board, into the same board or any other. Importing merges the file into the open board and sends it to everyone in the room through the usual encrypted sync. Like Export as PNG, the file is written to your device unencrypted, so anyone who gets hold of it can see the board: keep it somewhere safe or encrypt it before you pass it on.
whiteboard.about.7.title: Pictures
whiteboard.about.7: Drop a picture on the board, paste it or use Insert image in the toolbar. Your browser redraws it first: at most 1600 pixels on the long side, re-encoded as WebP, or JPEG where the browser cannot write WebP, at about 400 KB at most, which also strips metadata such as where a photo was taken. The picture is then embedded in the board itself and travels encrypted and signed like every stroke; it never goes to an upload service. A board holds up to 12 MB of pictures, and both PNG and board exports include them.
whiteboard.about.8.title: My rooms
whiteboard.about.8: Once you are on a board, Save to My rooms in the board menu adds it to a list shown on this page and on the chat page. It stays in this browser on this device and is never synced or sent anywhere. The board name, your label for it and the time of your last visit are stored as they are, like your browser history. The password is stored only encrypted with AES-256-GCM, under a key that HKDF-SHA256 derives from the WebAuthn PRF output of a passkey created for this list, so only that passkey, unlocked with your fingerprint, face, PIN or security key, can release it; the key stays in memory for the open page only. Without PRF support only names are kept. Forget removes one board; Forget everything removes the list and the passkey reference, while the passkey itself is deleted in your device or password manager.

chat.about.11.title: View-once, burn and scheduled messages
chat.about.11: A view-once message opens the first time anyone in the room taps it and then disappears for everyone, so in a room of three the first reader consumes it for all. Burning one of your own messages removes it for everyone: each member's browser drops its own copy once the burn arrives, and the relay never had one to drop. The burn travels as an encrypted message signed like any other, and it only counts when it comes from the same key that signed the message. A scheduled message waits in this browser only: it stays sealed under the room key in session storage, sends when its timer fires while this tab is open, retries for ten minutes if the room is offline and is then dropped with a notice. Closing the tab discards any scheduled sends.
rooms.passkeyExplain.title: What a passkey does here
rooms.passkeyExplain.body1: A passkey is a key that stays on your device. You unlock it with your fingerprint, face, PIN or security key — the same unlock you already use. You do not invent a new password for encrypt.click, and we never see that unlock.
rooms.passkeyExplain.body2: The room name stays as plain text, like a bookmark. The password or link is encrypted on this device first. Only a key derived from your passkey can open it. Nothing from that sealed secret is sent to encrypt.click.
rooms.passkeyExplain.body3: Someone who steals only the list still cannot read the passwords. They would need your device unlock as well. The wrapping key lives in memory for this page only and is wiped when you leave. That is stronger than saving the password in clear text in the browser.
rooms.passkeyExplain.tip: Prefer the unlock already on this device (Windows Hello, Touch ID, face or PIN). Some password apps create a passkey that cannot protect room secrets here — then only the name is saved.
tools.ultimateEncrypt.largeNotice.title: This file stays with you
tools.ultimateEncrypt.largeNotice.desc: Files over 128 MB are encrypted into a downloadable .enc file instead of a link. Send it to the recipient yourself — they open it on the decrypt page with the password.
tools.ultimateEncrypt.options.viewOnceHi: After the link is opened once in a browser, it will not open there again.
tools.ultimateEncrypt.options.deadManHin: The link stays sealed until the set time and then opens on its own, even if you are not there to send anything.
tools.ultimateEncrypt.options.deadManRes: Dead man's release: this link opens by itself at {time}. Send it now — nothing more is needed from you.
tools.ultimateEncrypt.offlineDropHint: A drop file is the sealed share as a small JSON file. Hand it over instead of the link — the recipient opens it on the decrypt page. It never contains the password.
